title: Personal Selling and Salesmanship

pattern.summary: 8 questions, attempt any 5, each carries 20 marks. All theory; Q8 is always 'short notes on any two of four'. Examiners ask for examples in almost every question.

choosing: The same questions repeat almost word for word: buyer behaviour factors, buying motives, sales reports, motivating salespeople, objection handling and closing techniques.
Q8 (any two short notes of four) is a safe pick — sales manual, prospecting and ethics come up again and again.
Almost every question says 'with examples' — give one Indian example (a product you know) in every point.

topics.name: Sales Reports, Documents & Sales Manual
topics.summary: Sales reports (objectives, features, types), documents salespeople prepare, sales manual, order book.
points: Sales reports record what salespeople do and achieve, and help managers plan, control and evaluate.

Types of documents: progress or call report (each call, orders, competing brands), sales work plan report (accounts, routes, travel ahead), expense report (for reimbursement), new business report, lost sales report, and complaints and adjustments report.
Features of a good report: accurate, timely, brief and clear, complete, in a standard format and factual.
Sales manual: a guide to the company's best policies, practices, procedures and standards for salespeople; a key training resource that must be kept up to date.
Order book: records orders taken — customer, items, quantity, price and delivery terms.

Cash memo: given by the seller when goods are sold for cash — date, serial number, names and addresses, description, rate, discount, tax, total in words and figures, signature. It differs from a money receipt, which only acknowledges cash received.
Tour diary: a small book of the sales visits made during a period — dates, places, purpose and results.
topics.frame: Meaning → objectives or contents as headed points → a sample format (columns of a call report) → benefits → conclusion.
examples:
Example: a day's call report
Date, territory, shops visited (8), orders booked (5 shops, ₹42,000), competing brands seen on display, a complaint about late delivery at one shop, and the plan for tomorrow. The manager uses these reports to check effort, spot problems and plan stock.

Example: cash memo
A customer buys two shirts for cash. The shop gives a cash memo showing its serial number and date, the shop's name and address, the items, rate, discount, GST and total in words and figures, signed by the seller. It serves as proof of purchase for an exchange or a warranty claim.

topics.name: Sales Presentation, Demonstration & Objections
topics.summary: Presentation and demonstration steps and strategies, and handling objections.
points: A sales presentation is a talk giving information about a product to persuade people to buy; a demonstration shows the product working.
Steps: attract attention → create interest → arouse desire → build conviction → get action.
Types of presentation: canned (memorised), organised and tailored (fitted to the customer).
Strategies: stimulus–response, AIDA, need identification and satisfaction, consultative selling, professional selling and depth selling.
Types of prospects: sceptical, procrastinator, silent, opinionated, talkative, timid and cautious, methodical, impulsive and 'chip on the shoulder' — each needs a different handling.

Methods of handling objections: 'yes, but' (indirect denial), counterbalance (offset a valid objection with an advantage), denial (firmly deny a wrong one), question method, failure-to-hear (deliberately ignore) and boomerang (turn the objection into a reason to buy).
Rules: never argue, pause before answering, don't over-answer, find out if you don't know, stay confident.
topics.frame: Meaning → steps or strategies as headed points, each with one product example → conclusion.
mistakes: Arguing with the prospect is itself a listed mistake — mention 'never argue' when writing on objections.
examples:
Example: AIDA in a mixer-grinder demonstration
Attention: grinds ice in 10 seconds in front of the customer. Interest: explains the three jars and the motor's warranty. Desire: lets the customer try making chutney. Conviction: shows reviews and the ISI mark. Action: 'I can deliver it today with a festival discount.'

Example: handling objections
'Your price is higher than the online price.' — Yes-but: 'Yes, it is ₹300 more, but you get free installation and a local service centre.'
Boomerang: 'I'm too busy to learn a new software.' — 'That's exactly why it helps: it saves you two hours a day.'
Counterbalance: 'It is heavier than others.' — 'It is, because of the copper motor, which lasts twice as long.'

topics.name: Motivating & Paying Salespeople
topics.summary: Role of motivation, Maslow's theory for salespeople, financial and non-financial techniques, compensation plans.
points: Motivation creates an urge in a person to reach a goal; a salesperson's motivation directly affects performance and targets.
Salespeople work alone, face rejection and irregular results, so they need more motivation than most staff.
Motivation is dynamic — needs change, and a satisfied need no longer motivates.
Maslow applied to salespeople: physiological (fair pay), safety (job security, insurance), social (team belonging), esteem (recognition, awards) and self-actualisation (challenging targets, growth).

Monetary rewards: salary, commission, bonus, incentives, contests, profit sharing, fringe benefits. Non-monetary: recognition, praise, promotion, training, participation in setting targets, sales meetings.

Compensation plans: straight salary (security, less push), straight commission (strong push, insecure) and combination plans (salary plus commission or bonus — most common). The right plan depends on the firm's nature and size and the length of the sales cycle.
topics.frame: Meaning → Maslow pyramid adapted to salespeople → financial vs non-financial table → conclusion.
examples:
Example: comparing compensation plans
A salesperson sells ₹8 lakh in a month.
Straight salary: ₹20,000 whatever the sales — secure, but little push to sell more.
Straight commission at 3%: ₹24,000 this month — strong push, but in a bad month earnings may fall close to nil.
Combination: ₹15,000 salary + 2% commission on sales above ₹5 lakh = 15,000 + 6,000 = ₹21,000 — security plus incentive, which is why it is the most common plan.

Example: Maslow for a sales team
Fair pay and travel allowance (physiological), health insurance and job security (safety), team outings (social), 'Salesperson of the Month' award (esteem), and a chance to open a new territory (self-actualisation).

topics.name: Buying Motives
topics.summary: Meaning, types and application of buying motives in personal selling.
points: A buying motive is the urge or reason that leads a customer to buy.
Two main types: product motives (why this product — size, colour, package, quality, design) and patronage motives (why from this seller).
Each is either rational (decided logically) or emotional (driven by feelings).
Rational product motives: safety or security, economy (low running cost), price, suitability, versatility, durability, convenience or comfort.
Emotional product motives: prestige or pride, emulation (copying others), affection, individuality, pleasure or recreation, habit.
Patronage motives: convenience, lower prices, credit facilities, wider choice, the shop's reputation and appearance, recommendations, emulation, prestige and habit.
Use in selling: find the prospect's dominant motive early, stress the benefit that matches it, and use it when handling objections and closing.
topics.frame: Meaning → types in a chart with an example each → how a salesperson uses them → conclusion.
examples:
Example: rational and emotional motives in one purchase
A family buys a car. Rational product motives: safety (airbags), economy (mileage) and durability. Emotional product motives: prestige (a well-known brand) and emulation (the neighbour has one). Patronage motive: they buy from a dealer they trust because of good after-sales service and easy finance.
A good salesperson finds the dominant motive — here safety, for the parents — and builds the presentation around it.

topics.name: Buyer Behaviour
topics.summary: Buyer vs consumer, factors affecting buyer behaviour, why understanding it matters.
points: Buyer behaviour: how people decide what, when, where and how to buy.
Buyer vs consumer: the buyer purchases; the consumer uses (a parent buys toys, the child uses them) — they may be the same person or different people.

Factors: cultural (culture, sub-culture, social class), social (family, reference groups, roles and status), personal (age, occupation, income, lifestyle, personality) and psychological (motivation, perception, learning, beliefs and attitudes).
Why a salesperson must know it: to spot needs, choose the right approach, expect objections, build lasting relationships and sell more.
topics.frame: Meaning → four factor groups as headings with examples → importance → conclusion.
examples:
Example: buyer vs consumer, and influences
A mother buys a school bag for her 8-year-old: she is the buyer, the child is the consumer, and the child's classmates (a reference group) influence which design is wanted. The mother's budget (personal) and her perception of which brand lasts longer (psychological) decide the final choice. A salesperson must satisfy both the child and the mother.

topics.name: Selling Process, Prospecting & Qualifying
topics.summary: Steps of the personal selling process; prospecting vs qualifying; types of prospects.
points: A sales process is the set of steps a salesperson follows to turn a prospect into a customer; it varies by industry (cars vs insurance).
Seven steps: prospecting and qualifying → pre-approach → approach → presentation or demonstration → handling objections → closing → follow-up.
Qualifying: a prospect must have the need, the authority, the ability (money) and the eligibility to buy.
Prospecting methods: centre of influence, spotters, advertising, endless chain (referrals), observation, cold canvassing, company records and retailers.
Pre-approach: learn the prospect's needs, behaviour, likes, preferences and status; it saves time by focusing on real prospects, not mere suspects.
Approach methods: introductory, customer-benefit, compliment, reference, interactive, dramatic and sample approach.
Objections are a sign of interest — a request for more information, time or assurance.
topics.frame: Meaning → flow chart of steps → one line and one example per step → conclusion.
examples:
Example: the seven steps in insurance selling
Prospecting: an agent gets names of newly married couples from existing clients (endless chain) and qualifies them — they need cover, can pay and decide themselves.
Pre-approach: learns about their jobs and family plans.
Approach: a reference approach — 'Your friend Ravi suggested I meet you.'
Presentation: shows how a term plan protects the family, with figures.
Objections: 'Premium is too high' → shows the cost per day.
Closing: 'Shall we start the policy from this month?'
Follow-up: helps with medical tests and sends a reminder before each premium.

topics.name: Salesmanship & Qualities of a Salesperson
topics.summary: Types of salesmanship, creative selling, role, qualities, duties and skills of a (modern) salesperson; careers.
points: Salesmanship is the art of persuading people to buy goods or services that satisfy their needs.

Types in the book: wholesaler's salesman; manufacturer's salesman (missionary, technical, merchandising, sales promotion); retailer's salesman (indoor and outdoor); specialty salesman (costly durables like cars, furniture, appliances).

Creative salesmanship creates demand for old and new products by arousing wants the buyer did not feel; the creative selling process runs from finding prospects and their needs to closing and follow-up.
Role of a salesperson: link between firm and customer, creates new customers, sells more to existing ones, solves problems, gives service and gathers market information.
Qualities: physical (health, appearance), mental (alertness, memory, imagination), social (courtesy, tact), character (honesty, loyalty) and knowledge of product, company and customer.

Why choose a sales career: earning potential, flexibility, job security, satisfaction, a stepping stone to management and in-demand skills. Big sales industries: IT, real estate, pharma, healthcare, food and financial services.
Changing role: with digital marketing and e-commerce the salesperson is becoming a trusted adviser and consultant, travelling less and using online audio and video calls more.
topics.frame: Definition → qualities or duties grouped under headings, with examples → conclusion.
examples:
Example: creative salesmanship
A water-purifier salesperson meets a family who buy bottled water and never thought of a purifier. By showing them a TDS test of their tap water and working out that the purifier pays for itself in a year compared with bottled water, the salesperson creates a want the family did not feel before.

Example: types of salesmen
A person selling a manufacturer's cement to dealers → manufacturer's salesman. One who explains a new medicine to doctors without taking orders → missionary salesman. An assistant at a clothes shop counter → retailer's indoor salesman. A car showroom executive → specialty salesman.

topics.name: Sales Management & Salesforce
topics.summary: Meaning, importance and scope of sales management; salesforce management process; recruitment, selection, training.
points: Sales is the only marketing function that brings revenue; salespeople are the link between the firm and its customers.
Sales management today means developing the sales staff, managing sales operations and using sales techniques so that targets are met.
Scope: sales forecasting and budgeting, sales team structure, manpower planning and hiring, training, sales territories and sales force management.
Sales management process: planning, organising, staffing, training, leading and controlling the sales force.
Trends: global markets, new technology, a diverse workforce, omni-channel management and e-selling.

Sales force management: recruitment planning → recruitment (sourcing candidates, internal and external, ends when applications are received) → selection (choosing the best from the applicants) → training → compensation → motivation → evaluation.
Training costs a lot but pays back — customers judge the firm by how well the salesperson demonstrates, handles objections and shows confidence.
Evaluation compares actual performance with objectives to find gaps and act in time; it also motivates by giving feedback.
topics.frame: Definition → process as a flow chart → one line per step → conclusion.
examples:
Example: the sales management process at a paint company
Planning: forecast next year's sales at ₹50 crore and split targets by region. Organising: divide the country into territories with an area manager for each. Staffing: recruit and select 30 new sales representatives. Training: product knowledge, colour consultation and handling objections. Leading: monthly meetings and incentives. Controlling: compare each territory's sales with its target and act on shortfalls.

topics.name: Personal Selling: Concept & Situations
topics.summary: Meaning, nature, characteristics and objectives of personal selling; selling situations; selling vs marketing.
points: Personal selling is the part of the promotion mix where a salesperson deals with the customer personally — face to face or online — in direct two-way communication, using words and body language. It is a 'push' strategy.
Characteristics: flexible (presentation fits the customer), engaging, builds relationships, quick response and feedback.
Use it for B2B selling, high-priced or technical products, new products that need explaining, a few large customers, serving middlemen, or when the advertising budget is small.

Advantages: two-way and flexible, sharp focus on target customers, personal attention, instant feedback, measurable results, extra non-selling tasks. Disadvantages: high cost, high staff turnover, message not standardised, salespeople differ in ability and motivation.

Qualitative objectives: find prospects, stimulate demand, serve and keep customers, collect market information, support middlemen, build brand image and goodwill. Quantitative (short-term): sales volume, product mix, expense limits, market share, number of new customers.
Selling functions: delivery salesperson, inside and outside order-takers, missionary salespeople, support staff (technical, merchandisers, customer service) and creative salespeople (order-getters).
Process: prospecting → preparation → approach → presentation → handling objections → closing → follow-up.
Selling vs marketing: selling is part of marketing — exchanging goods for a price; marketing starts with finding customer needs and ends with customer satisfaction and feedback.
topics.frame: Definition → characteristics as headed points → situations table with examples → conclusion.
examples:
Example: when personal selling is the right tool
A company making hospital ventilators sells to a few large hospitals. The product is costly and technical, and doctors have questions. A trained salesperson visits, demonstrates the machine, answers doubts on the spot, adjusts the offer (training, service contract) and follows up after installation. TV advertising would be wasteful here; two-way, face-to-face selling fits.

Example: order-taker vs order-getter
A salesperson who visits grocery shops every week to take repeat orders for biscuits is an order-taker. A salesperson who persuades a college to buy a new learning-management software it had never considered is a creative salesperson (order-getter).

topics.name: Closing the Sale
topics.summary: Closing techniques, trial close and closing cues.
points: Closing is the outcome of the whole selling process — getting the order after objections are answered. The salesperson must know both how and when to close.
Closing cues: buying signals such as questions on price, delivery or guarantee, handling the product closely, or nodding.

Trial close: a question used after the presentation to check if the prospect likes the product, whether objections are cleared and whether they are ready; if an indirect trial close fails, try a direct close.
Closing techniques in the book: choice, minor-point, assumptive, stimulus–response, summary, special-deal and turnover close.
Closing is not the end: follow-up calls calm the buyer's anxiety and start a long-term relationship (relationship marketing).
topics.frame: Meaning → techniques as headed points each with a one-line example dialogue → conclusion.
examples:
Example: buying signals and closing techniques
The customer asks, 'Does it come in blue, and how soon can you deliver?' — buying signals.
Choice close: 'Would you like the blue one or the grey one?' Assumptive close: 'I'll schedule delivery for Saturday.' Summary close: 'So you get the larger capacity, the 5-year warranty and free installation.' Special-deal close: 'The exchange offer ends today.'
After the sale, a follow-up call a week later reassures the buyer and opens the door to referrals.

topics.name: Ethics in Selling
topics.summary: Ethical and legal issues in selling, importance of ethics, sales code of conduct.
points: Ethics means values and principles of right and wrong; legal issues are those set by government law. Some unethical selling is also illegal.
Common issues: misrepresenting or hiding facts, price discrimination, bribes, tie-in sales, false promises or exaggeration (puffery) and invasion of privacy.
Bribes are covered by the Contract Act, 1872 and the Sale of Goods Act, 1930.
Pressure to meet targets is the main reason salespeople take shortcuts.
Compliance techniques: hire the right salespeople, set a code of conduct for ethical selling, train people in ethical selling, and avoid exaggerated or unverified claims.
Why it matters: customer trust, long-term relationships, company reputation and avoiding legal trouble.
topics.frame: Meaning → issues grouped by stakeholder with examples → legal angle → conclusion.
examples:
Example: ethical or not?
Telling a customer that a phone is waterproof when it is only splash-resistant → misrepresentation (unethical, and may be illegal). Saying 'our best phone ever!' → puffery, mild, but claims should not be misleading. Offering a purchase officer a gift to win a large order → a bribe. Selling a customer's phone number to another company → invasion of privacy.
A firm prevents such behaviour through a code of conduct, training, and targets that do not push staff to cut corners.
